title: AP Statistics
subject: AP Statistics
blurb: Interpret data, designs, probabilities and inference the way the AP exam asks you to.

rounds.title: Round 1: Exploring data
rounds.intro: Distributions, z-scores, transformations and regression. Show your work, not just your memory.

questions.q: Using the 1.5 × IQR rule, which of the extreme values are outliers?
questions.scene: Quiz scores have Q1 = 42 and Q3 = 58. The most extreme values in the data set are 15, 19, 81 and 84; all other scores lie between 30 and 70.
choices: All four extreme values
15 and 84 only
84 only
None, since all four are within 1.5 IQR of the median
questions.why: IQR = 16, so the fences are 42 - 24 = 18 and 58 + 24 = 82. 15 is below 18 and 84 is above 82; 19 and 81 are inside. The trap is measuring from the median instead of the quartiles.

questions.q: Who did better relative to their own class?
questions.scene: Maya scored 84 on an exam with mean 72 and SD 8. Jon scored 74 on a different exam with mean 65 and SD 5.
choices: Maya: 84 is a higher raw score than 74
Maya: her exam had the larger SD, so it was harder to beat
Jon: his z-score is 1.8 versus Maya's 1.5
They tie, since both scored above their class mean
questions.why: Maya: z = (84-72)/8 = 1.5. Jon: z = (74-65)/5 = 1.8. Raw scores from different distributions can't be compared; standardize first.

questions.q: What are the mean and SD of the temperatures in °F?
questions.scene: Daily temperatures in °C have mean 20 and SD 4. They are converted with F = 1.8C + 32.
choices: Mean 52, SD 7.2
Mean 68, SD 4
Mean 68, SD 39.2
Mean 68, SD 7.2
questions.why: Multiplying by 1.8 scales the mean and SD: mean = 1.8(20)+32 = 68, SD = 1.8(4) = 7.2. Adding 32 shifts the center but never changes the spread, so SD 39.2 is the trap.

questions.q: Which is the best interpretation of the slope?
questions.scene: A regression of exam score (points) on weekly study time (hours) gives ŷ = 25 + 3.2x.
choices: Each extra hour of weekly study is associated with a predicted increase of 3.2 points
Studying one more hour will cause a 3.2-point gain
Each extra point goes with 3.2 more hours of studying
A student who studies 0 hours is predicted to score 3.2
questions.why: The slope is the predicted change in y per one-unit increase in x. It describes association, not cause, and the units are points per hour, not hours per point.

questions.q: What is the residual for this student, and what does it mean?
questions.scene: A fitted line is ŷ = 40 + 2.5x. A student with x = 10 actually has y = 61.
choices: +4; the line underestimates this student's y by 4
-4; the line underestimates this student's y by 4
-4; the line overestimates this student's y by 4
+21; the student is 21 above the line
questions.why: Predicted = 40 + 25 = 65, and residual = actual - predicted = 61 - 65 = -4. Negative means the point sits below the line, so the line overpredicts. Subtracting in the wrong order flips the sign.

questions.q: Which statement is correct?
questions.scene: In a sample of 60 students, the correlation between daily TV hours and GPA is r = -0.80.
choices: About 64% of the variation in GPA is accounted for by the linear relationship with TV hours
About 80% of the variation in GPA is explained by TV hours
About 64% of students fall exactly on the regression line
Each extra TV hour causes a 64% drop in GPA
questions.why: r² = (-0.80)² = 0.64, the fraction of variation in y explained by the linear model. Using r instead of r² is the common slip, and no correlation proves cause.

questions.q: What are the new correlation and slope?
questions.scene: Heights (inches) and weights (pounds) of players have r = 0.70, and the least-squares slope is 4 lb per inch. All heights are converted to centimeters (1 in = 2.54 cm); weights stay in pounds.
choices: r = 0.70, slope = 10.16 lb per cm
r ≈ 0.28, slope = 4 lb per cm
r = 0.70, slope = 4 lb per cm
r = 0.70, slope ≈ 1.57 lb per cm
questions.why: Correlation has no units and is unchanged by linear rescaling. The slope is lb per unit of x, and one cm is smaller than one inch, so slope = 4/2.54 ≈ 1.57. Multiplying by 2.54 is the trap.

questions.q: What is the predicted y when x = 70?
questions.scene: For a sample, x̄ = 50, sx = 10, ȳ = 200, sy = 30 and r = 0.60.
questions.why: Slope b = r(sy/sx) = 0.6(30/10) = 1.8, so ŷ = 200 + 1.8(70-50) = 236. 260 assumes x being 2 SDs above means y is also 2 SDs above, ignoring that r < 1 pulls the prediction toward the mean.

rounds.title: Round 2: Collecting data
rounds.intro: Sampling, bias, experiments and what you are allowed to conclude.

questions.q: What sampling method is this?
questions.scene: A principal wants to survey students. She randomly picks 5 of the 20 homerooms and surveys every student in those 5 rooms.
choices: Cluster sample
Stratified random sample
Simple random sample
Systematic sample
questions.why: The homerooms are clusters, a few are chosen at random, and everyone in them is surveyed. Stratified would sample some students from every group; an SRS would give every set of students an equal chance, which this does not.

questions.q: What is the main concern about trusting 78% as the city's support?
questions.scene: A city mails a survey about a new tax to 2000 randomly chosen households. 340 are returned, and 78% of those favor the tax.
choices: Undercoverage, because the sample was random
Response bias from leading question wording
Sampling variability, which random selection removes
Nonresponse bias: people who return mail surveys may differ from those who don't
questions.why: Only 17% responded, and responders often feel strongly, so the results may not reflect the 2000 chosen. Random selection does not fix this, and sampling variability is not bias.

questions.q: Which conclusion is justified?
questions.scene: Researchers examine health records and find that adults who take vitamin D supplements have fewer fractures than adults who do not.
choices: Vitamin D supplements reduce fractures
Vitamin D is associated with fewer fractures, but confounding (e.g. healthier habits) may explain it
The relationship is probably due to chance since no p-value was given
Nothing, because records are not a random sample
questions.why: No treatment was assigned, so this is observational. People choosing supplements may also exercise more or eat better, which confounds. Only random assignment supports a causal claim.

questions.q: Why should she block by field?
questions.scene: An agronomist tests two fertilizers on 40 plots. Twenty plots are in a sandy field and twenty in a clay field, and soil strongly affects yield.
choices: So she no longer needs random assignment
To make the sample large enough to generalize to all farms
To remove soil-type variability from the comparison, with random assignment of fertilizers within each field
To make the two fertilizer groups blind to the treatment
questions.why: Blocking groups similar units so differences between fertilizers are not muddied by soil. Randomization still happens inside each block. Blocking is about reducing variability, not about replacing randomization.

questions.q: What can reasonably be concluded?
questions.scene: A study of 80 volunteers at one college randomly assigns half to a new sleep routine; the routine group shows significantly better memory scores.
choices: The routine improves memory for all adults
The routine is only associated with better memory, since subjects volunteered
The result is meaningless because the groups were not random samples
The routine caused improved memory in volunteers like these, but generalizing wider is risky
questions.why: Random assignment allows cause and effect within the study. Volunteers were not randomly selected, so inference to a larger population is limited. Volunteering affects scope, not causation.

questions.q: Why is the coin flip for order important?
questions.scene: Each of 24 runners tries both brand X and brand Y shoes on a 5 km course, with the order decided by a coin flip for each runner.
choices: It makes the sample a simple random sample of runners
It keeps order effects such as fatigue or practice from being confounded with brand
It guarantees the runners cannot tell which brand is which
It makes a two-sample test appropriate
questions.why: If everyone wore X first, a fatigue advantage for Y would be tangled with brand. Random order spreads that effect evenly. This is a matched-pairs design, so the analysis is on differences, not two independent groups.

questions.q: About how large must the sample be to get a margin of error of 2 points?
questions.scene: A poll of n = 600 voters has a margin of error of 4 percentage points at 95% confidence.
questions.why: ME is proportional to 1/√n, so halving it requires 4 times the sample: 600 × 4 = 2400. Doubling n only cuts ME by a factor of 1/√2, the usual mistake.

questions.q: Which conclusion is best supported?
questions.scene: A researcher randomly samples 500 households in a city; 320 agree to take part. The 320 are randomly assigned to get a free smart thermostat or not, and the thermostat group uses significantly less energy.
choices: Thermostats cause lower use among households willing to participate; nonresponse limits generalizing to the whole city
Thermostats cause lower use in all city households, since both selection and assignment were random
Only an association exists, because households chose whether to take part
Nothing can be concluded unless households were blind to their thermostat
questions.why: Random assignment supports causation. But the initial random sample was damaged by 36% nonresponse, so the participants are effectively volunteers. Blinding isn't possible here and doesn't void the result.

rounds.title: Round 3: Probability and random variables
rounds.intro: Conditional probability, distributions, combining variables and sampling distributions.

questions.q: A randomly chosen student owns a laptop. What is the probability they take AP?
questions.scene: 30% of students take AP. Of AP students, 80% own a laptop; of non-AP students, 50% do.
questions.why: P(AP and laptop) = 0.3(0.8) = 0.24 and P(laptop) = 0.24 + 0.7(0.5) = 0.59, so P(AP | laptop) = 0.24/0.59 ≈ 0.407. 0.80 is P(laptop | AP), the reversed condition.

questions.q: Which statement is true about A and B?
choices: They are independent but not mutually exclusive
They are mutually exclusive
They are both independent and mutually exclusive
They are neither independent nor mutually exclusive
questions.why: P(A and B) = 0.4 + 0.5 - 0.7 = 0.2 = (0.4)(0.5), so they are independent. Since P(A and B) is not 0 they are not mutually exclusive; in fact, mutually exclusive events with positive probability can never be independent.

questions.q: What is the probability she makes at least 8?
questions.scene: A basketball player makes each free throw with probability 0.7, independently. She shoots 10.
questions.why: P(8) = 45(0.7)^8(0.3)^2 ≈ 0.233, P(9) ≈ 0.121, P(10) ≈ 0.028, which add to ≈ 0.383. 0.233 is only exactly 8; 0.617 is the complement, P(at most 7).

questions.q: What is the probability the first success occurs on exactly the 4th trial?
questions.scene: Each trial of an experiment succeeds with probability 0.2, independently. Trials are repeated until the first success.
questions.why: Geometric: three failures then a success, 0.8³ × 0.2 = 0.1024. 0.8⁴ is the chance of four failures, and 0.8⁴(0.2) would put the success on trial 5.

questions.q: What are the mean and SD of D?
questions.scene: Independent random variables: X has mean 50 and SD 6; Y has mean 40 and SD 8. Let D = X - Y.
choices: Mean 10, SD 10
Mean 10, SD 2
Mean 10, SD 14
Mean 90, SD 10
questions.why: Means subtract: 50 - 40 = 10. Variances add, even for a difference: 36 + 64 = 100, so SD = 10. Subtracting SDs (2) or adding them (14) is the classic error.

questions.q: Approximately what is P(p̂ ≥ 0.40)?
questions.scene: The true proportion of voters favoring a measure is p = 0.30. A random sample of n = 100 is taken.
questions.why: SD of p̂ = √(0.3·0.7/100) ≈ 0.0458, so z = 0.10/0.0458 ≈ 2.18 and the tail is ≈ 0.015. Using SD 0.05 gives 0.023, and using SD 0.10 gives 0.159; np = 30 and n(1-p) = 70 both exceed 10, so Normal is fine.

questions.q: Which describes the sampling distribution of x̄?
questions.scene: A population is strongly right-skewed with mean 20 and SD 15. Samples of n = 36 are drawn and x̄ is recorded each time.
choices: Mean 20, SD 15, right-skewed like the population
Mean 20, SD 2.5, approximately Normal
Mean 20, SD 2.5, right-skewed like the population
Mean 3.33, SD 2.5, approximately Normal
questions.why: The mean of x̄ is μ = 20 and the SD is σ/√n = 15/6 = 2.5. With n = 36 the CLT makes x̄ roughly Normal despite the skewed population. The sampling distribution is not the population distribution.

questions.q: What are the mean and SD of the total payout?
questions.scene: A policy pays $0 with probability 0.90, $1000 with probability 0.08 and $5000 with probability 0.02. An insurer sells 100 independent policies.
choices: Mean $180, SD $740
questions.why: Per policy: mean = 80 + 100 = 180; E(X²) = 580,000 so variance = 580,000 - 180² = 547,600 and SD = 740. For 100 policies, mean = 18,000 and SD = 740√100 = 7,400. SDs scale by √n, not n.

rounds.title: Round 4: Inference
rounds.intro: Intervals, tests, errors, chi-square and picking the right procedure.

questions.q: Which interpretation is correct?
questions.scene: A 95% confidence interval for mean commute time, based on a random sample of 50 workers, is (22.1, 26.9) minutes.
choices: There is a 95% probability the true mean lies in (22.1, 26.9)
95% of workers have commutes between 22.1 and 26.9 minutes
95% of sample means fall between 22.1 and 26.9
If we repeated the sampling many times, about 95% of such intervals would contain the true mean
questions.why: Confidence is about the method's long-run capture rate. The true mean is fixed, so this one interval either contains it or doesn't. The interval is for μ, not for individual commutes.

questions.q: What does the p-value 0.03 mean?
questions.scene: A test of H0: p = 0.5 versus Ha: p > 0.5 gives a p-value of 0.03.
choices: If p were truly 0.5, a sample result this extreme or more would occur about 3% of the time
There is a 3% chance that H0 is true
There is a 97% chance that Ha is true
The result happened by chance 3% of the time
questions.why: The p-value is P(data this extreme | H0 true), not the probability H0 is true. Hypotheses are about fixed parameters, so they get no probability from a frequentist test.

questions.q: Which change increases power without raising the Type I error rate?
questions.scene: A company tests a drug at α = 0.05 with n = 50 per group.
choices: Increase α to 0.10
Decrease α to 0.01
Use a smaller sample to reduce variability
Increase the sample size to n = 200 per group
questions.why: Larger n shrinks the SE, making it easier to detect a true difference while α stays 0.05. Raising α also increases power but raises Type I error; lowering α reduces power.

questions.q: What is the test result for H0: the die is fair?
questions.scene: A die is rolled 120 times. Counts for faces 1 to 6 are 15, 25, 20, 22, 18, 20.
choices: χ² = 2.9 with df = 6; no convincing evidence
χ² = 58 with df = 5; reject H0
χ² = 2.9 with df = 5; no convincing evidence the die is unfair
χ² = 2.9 with df = 5; reject H0
questions.why: Expected = 20 each; χ² = (25+25+0+4+4+0)/20 = 2.9. df = 6 - 1 = 5 and the 0.05 critical value is 11.07, far above 2.9. Forgetting to divide by expected gives 58.

questions.q: What is the 95% confidence interval for the true slope? (t* for df = 20 is 2.086)
questions.scene: Computer output for a regression based on n = 22 data points: slope coefficient 0.48 with SE 0.15 (t = 3.20, P = 0.005); R-sq = 36.4%.
questions.why: df = n - 2 = 20, margin = 2.086(0.15) ≈ 0.313, giving 0.48 ± 0.313. Using z = 1.96 narrows it to (0.19, 0.77); using only ±SE gives (0.33, 0.63).

questions.q: Which procedure is appropriate?
questions.scene: 25 patients have blood pressure measured before and after a month on a new diet. The researcher wants to know if the diet lowers mean pressure.
choices: Two-sample t-test comparing before and after groups
Two-proportion z-test
One-sample t-test on the 25 before-minus-after differences
Chi-square test of homogeneity
questions.why: The same patients appear in both measurements, so the data are paired. Analyze the differences, which removes patient-to-patient variability. A two-sample test wrongly treats the groups as independent.

questions.q: What is the test statistic?
questions.scene: Group A: 45 successes out of 100. Group B: 30 successes out of 100. We test H0: pA = pB versus Ha: pA ≠ pB.
choices: z ≈ 2.19 (using the pooled proportion 0.375)
z ≈ 2.22 (using unpooled standard error)
questions.why: Under H0 use pooled p̂ = 75/200 = 0.375, so SE = √(0.375·0.625·(1/100+1/100)) ≈ 0.0685 and z = 0.15/0.0685 ≈ 2.19. Unpooled SE is for confidence intervals; 3.10 drops the second sample.

questions.q: Approximately what is the power of the test?
questions.scene: Test H0: p = 0.5 versus Ha: p > 0.5 at α = 0.05 with n = 100. Suppose the truth is p = 0.6.
questions.why: Reject if p̂ > 0.5 + 1.645(0.05) ≈ 0.582. With p = 0.6, SD = √(0.24/100) ≈ 0.049, z = (0.582 - 0.6)/0.049 ≈ -0.36, so power = P(z > -0.36) ≈ 0.64. The 0.36 is β, the Type II error probability, which is the complement.
